type: viewpoint — true formally, not in reality
position: after its word — right after the title or noun (*a leader in name only*)
modifies: a noun or a whole predicate

senses.gloss: Officially or by title, but not in fact.
examples: He's the CEO *in name only*; his sister actually runs the company.
For their last ten years they were married *in name only*.
The ceasefire existed *in name only*.

type: time — very soon or very quickly
modifies: a verb or a whole clause

senses.gloss: Very quickly; almost immediately.
examples: Don't worry, we'll be there *in no time*.
She picked up Spanish *in no time*.
With four of us helping, the job was done *in no time*.

ru: сам по себе, по собственным заслугам
type: viewpoint — independently, on one's own merits
position: end — the possessive changes with the subject: *in her own right*, *in its own right*

senses.gloss: Because of one's own qualities or position, not because of a connection to someone or something else.
examples: Her father was famous, but she's a respected scientist *in her own right*.
The side dishes are worth the trip *in their own right*.
Once a small suburb, the town is now a city *in its own right*.

type: linking — restating something more simply or plainly

senses.gloss: Put another way; that is to say.
examples: The flight is overbooked. *In other words*, some of us won't get on.
He said he'd think about it — *in other words*, no.
So, *in other words*, you forgot.

type: focusing — singling out one item from a group
position: after its word — right after the noun it picks out (*one student in particular*), or at the end
modifies: a noun phrase or a whole clause
contrast: *Particularly* goes before its word (*particularly good*); *in particular* follows it (*this one in particular*). *Nothing in particular* = ничего особенного.

senses.gloss: Especially; more than the others.
examples: I loved the whole menu, but the desserts *in particular* were amazing.
Is there anything *in particular* you'd like to see?
Crime has fallen across the city, car thefts *in particular*.

type: manner — briefly, as a side remark

senses.gloss: Briefly, while talking or writing about something else.
examples: She mentioned *in passing* that she'd quit her job.
The book refers to the war only *in passing*.
I met him once, *in passing*, at a conference.

type: manner — physically present, face to face
contrast: Russian *лично* covers two English words. *In person* means physically present: *I spoke to her in person* (face to face). *Personally* gives an opinion: *Personally, I think it's a mistake* (лично я считаю).

senses.gloss: Physically present, not by phone, mail or online.
examples: You have to apply *in person* at the DMV.
She looks taller *in person* than on TV.
We've emailed for years but never met *in person*.

type: place — in position; also a state of being set up
contrast: *In place of* is a preposition meaning *instead of* (вместо): *She went in place of her boss*. *Out of place* = неуместный. Americans *run in place*; British English says *run on the spot*.

senses.gloss: In the right or usual position; not moving.
examples: Hold the shelf *in place* while I drill.
A few bobby pins kept her hat *in place*.
The coach had us jog *in place* to warm up.

senses.gloss: Set up and working; in effect.
examples: The new security rules are already *in place*.
We need a plan *in place* before hurricane season.

type: viewpoint — what actually happens, as opposed to theory
contrast: *Out of practice* means no longer skilled because of lack of training (потерял навык).

senses.gloss: In what really happens, as opposed to what should happen.
examples: The law sounds fair, but *in practice* it's rarely enforced.
*In practice*, most customers never read the terms.
It works on paper; *in practice*, not so much.

type: viewpoint — in general terms, before the details
modifies: a verb or a whole clause
contrast: A false friend. Russian *в принципе* often means *basically* or *generally speaking* (*В принципе, я свободен* = *Basically, I'm free*). English *in principle* means *as an idea, though not yet in practice or in detail*: *They agreed in principle* = they accepted the idea, details still to come. Don't confuse *principle* with *principal*.

senses.gloss: As a general idea, though the details or practice may be different.
examples: The board has agreed *in principle*, but the details still need work.
*In principle*, anyone can apply; in reality, few are accepted.
I'm not against the idea *in principle*.

type: manner — without other people present

senses.gloss: Without other people watching or listening.
examples: Can I talk to you *in private* for a minute?
The committee met *in private* before the vote.
Praise people in public and criticize them *in private*.

type: manner — where other people can see or hear

senses.gloss: Where other people can see or hear.
examples: He hates speaking *in public*.
She hasn't been seen *in public* since the scandal.
Please don't argue with me *in public*.

type: viewpoint — contrasting how things seem with how they are

senses.gloss: Actually, as opposed to how something seems or was expected to be.
examples: The job sounded glamorous; *in reality*, it was mostly paperwork.
*In reality*, few people read the fine print.
They seem rich, but *in reality* they're deep in debt.

type: manner — as an exchange or a response
modifies: a verb or a whole clause
contrast: With a noun it becomes *in return for*: *in return for your help*. Don't confuse with *in turn* (по очереди; в свою очередь).

senses.gloss: As a way of paying back or answering something someone did.
examples: I helped him move, and *in return* he fixed my car.
What do you want *in return*?
She smiled, and he smiled *in return*.

type: manner — without others knowing

senses.gloss: Without other people knowing.
examples: The two companies had been negotiating *in secret* for months.
They got married *in secret* in Las Vegas.
He practiced the speech *in secret* so no one would laugh.

type: linking — summing up
contrast: Not the same as *shortly*, which means *soon* (скоро). In casual speech Americans also say *long story short*.

senses.gloss: To sum up in a few words.
examples: The hotel was dirty, loud and overpriced. *In short*, avoid it.
*In short*, we need more money.
He's smart, reliable and kind — *in short*, the perfect hire.

type: time — quickly and without delay

senses.gloss: Quickly; without delay.
examples: The police arrived *in short order*.
The new owners replaced the entire staff *in short order*.
Once the parts came in, the mechanic had the car fixed *in short order*.

type: degree — to a very great extent; informal
modifies: a verb or a noun it follows (*talent in spades*)

senses.gloss: In large amounts; to a very high degree.
examples: She has talent *in spades*.
He paid me back *in spades*.
The movie promised action, and it delivered *in spades*.

type: manner — calmly, without being upset
position: end — almost always in *take something in stride*
contrast: American usage; British English says *take something in one's stride*.

senses.gloss: Calmly, without letting a problem upset or stop you.
examples: She took the bad news *in stride*.
Rookies often panic under pressure, but he takes it all *in stride*.
The kids took the move to a new city *in stride*.

type: manner — together, at the same time

senses.gloss: Together, or at the same time as something else.
examples: The two departments work *in tandem* on product launches.
Prices and wages rose *in tandem*.
The drug works best *in tandem* with physical therapy.

type: time — at first, in contrast to later
contrast: Russian *в начале* covers two English phrases. *In the beginning* = at first, before things changed (поначалу). *At the beginning of* + noun marks the start of something named: *at the beginning of the movie*, not *in the beginning of the movie*. The same split applies to *in the end* / *at the end of*.

senses.gloss: At first; at the start, before things changed.
examples: *In the beginning*, I hated living in the city.
It was hard *in the beginning*, but it gets easier.
*In the beginning* we had no customers at all.

type: time — finally, after everything; also linking
contrast: *In the end* = finally, after a process (в итоге). *At the end (of)* = at the last point of something: *at the end of the street*, *at the end of the movie*. *In the end of the movie* is a common mistake.

senses.gloss: Finally, after a long process or a lot of discussion.
examples: We argued for an hour, but *in the end* we ordered pizza.
*In the end*, it's your decision.
It was a tough season, but they won the title *in the end*.

type: time — originally, to begin with; also linking
position: end — for *originally*; front when listing reasons
contrast: The end-position use (*Why did you go there in the first place?*) is far more common than the list use, and Russian *во-первых* does not cover it; think *вообще* or *с самого начала*.

senses.gloss: At the very beginning; at all — usually when asking or complaining about why something happened.
examples: Why did you agree to it *in the first place*?
If you hadn't lied *in the first place*, we wouldn't be in this mess.
I never wanted to come *in the first place*.

senses.gloss: First of all, as the first in a list of reasons.
examples: *In the first place*, we can't afford it; in the second place, we don't need it.
*In the first place*, the report is late.

type: degree — used with a negative
position: before its word — or end (*Not in the least*)
modifies: an adjective, a verb, or a whole negative clause

senses.gloss: At all; even slightly — after *not* or another negative.
examples: I'm not *in the least* worried.
“Did the delay bother you?” “Not *in the least*.”
She didn't seem *in the least* surprised.

ru: в конечном счёте, в долгосрочной перспективе
type: time — over a long period, eventually
contrast: The opposite is *in the short run* or *in the short term*.

senses.gloss: Over a long period of time; eventually.
examples: Buying good boots saves money *in the long run*.
*In the long run*, the new highway will ease traffic.
It's painful now, but it'll be better for everyone *in the long run*.

type: manner — without help when help is needed
position: end — almost always in *leave someone in the lurch*

senses.gloss: In a difficult situation without the help someone was counting on.
examples: Our babysitter canceled at the last minute and left us *in the lurch*.
The contractor quit halfway through, leaving the owners *in the lurch*.
I won't leave you *in the lurch* — I'll finish before I go.

type: time — during the period until something happens

senses.gloss: During the time before something expected happens.
examples: The doctor will see you soon. *In the meantime*, please fill out this form.
Our new place isn't ready, so we're staying with friends *in the meantime*.
*In the meantime*, keep an eye on the weather.

ru: в последний момент, как раз вовремя
type: time — just before it is too late

senses.gloss: At the last possible moment; just before it is too late.
senses.ru: в последний момент, в самый раз
examples: The firefighters arrived *in the nick of time*.
I made the train *in the nick of time*.
She hit the brakes *in the nick of time*.

type: time — at the same moment, usually of contradictory statements

senses.gloss: At the same moment — used when two statements contradict each other, or when two things are wrongly treated as equal.
senses.ru: тут же, на одном дыхании, в одном ряду
examples: He said he trusted me and, *in the same breath*, asked to see my receipts.
You can't praise the plan and criticize it *in the same breath*.
His name shouldn't be mentioned *in the same breath* as the great players.

type: viewpoint — how things should work, as opposed to practice

senses.gloss: According to what should happen, though reality may be different.
examples: *In theory*, the train takes two hours.
It sounds great *in theory*, but will it work?
*In theory*, anyone can become president.

type: time
modifies: a verb or a whole clause; often *in time for* + noun or *in time to* + verb
contrast: Russian *вовремя* covers two English phrases. *On time* = at the scheduled moment, not late: *The train left on time*. *In time* = early enough for something: *We arrived in time to get seats*.

senses.gloss: Early enough; before it is too late.
examples: We got to the airport *in time* for our flight.
Will the package arrive *in time* for Christmas?
The ambulance got there just *in time*.

senses.gloss: Eventually; after enough time has passed.
examples: *In time*, you'll forget all about him.
The pain will fade *in time*.

ru: по правде говоря, на самом деле
type: stance — admitting what is really true
contrast: Somewhat formal and written; in speech Americans say *to tell the truth*, *honestly* or *actually*.

senses.gloss: Really; as is actually the case.
examples: He said he was fine, but *in truth* he was terrified.
*In truth*, I never liked the place.
The deal was, *in truth*, a disaster.

type: linking; also manner
modifies: a verb or a whole clause
contrast: *Take turns* is the usual way to say *делать по очереди*: *We took turns driving*. Don't confuse *in turn* with *in return* (взамен).

senses.gloss: As a result of that, in a chain of causes and effects.
examples: Higher gas prices raise shipping costs, which *in turn* raise food prices.
She trained the managers, who *in turn* trained their teams.
He was kind to me, and I, *in turn*, tried to help others.

senses.gloss: One after another, in order.
examples: The students spoke *in turn* about their projects.
She looked at each of us *in turn*.

type: manner — together, at the same time

senses.gloss: At the same moment, saying or doing the same thing.
examples: The class answered *in unison*.
The dancers moved *in unison*.
“Happy birthday!” they shouted *in unison*.

senses.gloss: In complete agreement.
examples: The allies acted *in unison* against the threat.
Both parties voted *in unison* for the bill.

type: manner — without success
modifies: a verb; also after *be* (*it was all in vain*)
contrast: The adjective *vain* means conceited (тщеславный); *in vain* is only about wasted effort. *Take someone's name in vain* = speak of them disrespectfully.

senses.gloss: Without success; with no result.
examples: We searched *in vain* for the keys.
The doctors tried *in vain* to save him.
All our hard work was *in vain*.

type: manner — as a written document

senses.gloss: Written down, especially as an official record.
examples: Can you give me that offer *in writing*?
All complaints must be submitted *in writing*.
Get the landlord's promise *in writing*.

type: manner; also degree
contrast: *Inside out* = наизнанку; *upside down* = вверх ногами; *backwards* (British *back to front*) = задом наперёд.

senses.gloss: With the inner side turned to the outside.
examples: You've got your sweater on *inside out*.
Turn the jeans *inside out* before you wash them.
The wind blew my umbrella *inside out*.

senses.gloss: Thoroughly, in every detail.
examples: She knows the tax code *inside out*.
After ten years there, he knew the building *inside out*.

type: degree — almost
contrast: *Just about to* + verb is different: *about to* means вот-вот, and *just* strengthens it (*The movie is just about to start*).

senses.gloss: Almost; very nearly.
examples: I'm *just about* ready — give me two minutes.
*Just about* everyone was there.
We've tried *just about* everything.

type: manner — as a precaution
contrast: At the end of a clause it is an adverb (*Take an umbrella, just in case*). Followed by a clause it is a conjunction (*Take an umbrella just in case it rains* = на случай, если). It is not *if*: *in case it rains* means as a precaution against rain, not on condition that it rains.

senses.gloss: As a precaution, because something might happen.
examples: Take an umbrella, *just in case*.
I made extra food *just in case*.
Write down my number, *just in case*.

type: time
contrast: In American English *just now* usually means *a moment ago* and takes the simple past (*I saw him just now*, not *I have seen him just now*). For the present Americans more often say *right now*.

senses.gloss: A moment ago.
examples: Who was that on the phone *just now*?
I saw her in the hallway *just now*.
What did you say *just now*?

senses.gloss: At this moment; right now.
examples: I'm busy *just now* — can I call you back?
She's not in the office *just now*.

ru: в этот самый момент, как раз тогда
type: time — at that exact moment in a past story
modifies: a whole clause, usually in the past tense
contrast: *Just then* points to a moment in a story (в этот момент); *just now* usually means a moment ago, measured from the present (только что).

senses.gloss: At exactly that moment, often when something unexpected happened.
senses.ru: в этот самый момент, как раз тогда
examples: I was about to leave, and *just then* the phone rang.
*Just then*, the lights went out.
She walked in *just then* and heard everything.

type: degree — a downtoner; informal
form: the noun *kind* + *of*, fused; often spelled *kinda* in casual writing
contrast: It is an adverb only before a verb, adjective or adverb (*I'm kind of tired*). Before a noun it is the noun *kind* + *of* (*What kind of car?* = какая машина). *Sort of* works the same way.

senses.gloss: Somewhat; a little; in a way.
examples: I'm *kind of* tired — can we go home?
The movie was *kind of* boring.
I *kind of* hoped you'd call.

ru: последний по порядку, но не по значению
type: linking — introducing the final item in a list
modifies: a whole clause or the last item in a list

senses.gloss: Mentioned last, but just as important as the others.
senses.ru: последний по порядку, но не по значению
examples: *Last but not least*, I want to thank my parents.
And *last but not least*, our drummer, Kevin!
Bring sunscreen, water and, *last but not least*, your ticket.

type: time — at a later point
modifies: a verb or a whole clause

senses.gloss: At a later time; afterward.
examples: I'll explain it to you *later on*.
*Later on*, she moved to Chicago.
We'll deal with that problem *later on* in the course.

ru: меньше всего, и уж точно не
type: focusing — after a negative, picking out the least likely case
position: after its word — after the negative statement, before the person or thing picked out
modifies: a noun phrase added to a negative statement

senses.gloss: Especially not; less than anyone or anything else.
examples: Nobody was happy with the result, *least of all* the coach.
I don't want to hurt anyone, *least of all* you.
No one expected her to win, *least of all* herself.

ru: не говоря уже о, тем более
type: linking — adds a stronger case after a negative
position: end — after a negative clause, before the stronger case
modifies: a noun, verb or phrase added to a negative statement
contrast: Used only after a negative or near-negative: *I can't boil an egg, let alone cook dinner*. After a positive statement use *not to mention*. Don't confuse with *leave someone alone* (оставить в покое).

senses.gloss: And certainly not — introducing something even less likely than what was just denied.
senses.ru: не говоря уже о, тем более
examples: I can't afford a car, *let alone* a house.
He can barely walk, *let alone* run a marathon.
Most people have never heard of the town, *let alone* visited it.

type: manner — smoothly and regularly

senses.gloss: Smoothly, regularly and exactly as planned.
examples: The whole event went off *like clockwork*.
Every morning at six, *like clockwork*, the neighbor's dog starts barking.
Her paycheck arrives *like clockwork* on the first of the month.

ru: как сумасшедший, бешено, изо всех сил
type: degree — very much, very hard; informal

senses.gloss: Very much, very fast or very hard.
examples: We had to work *like crazy* to finish on time.
It's been raining *like crazy* all week.
Tickets are selling *like crazy*.

ru: чертовски, изо всех сил; чёрта с два
type: degree; also negative
position: end — front in the refusal sense
modifies: a verb; in the refusal sense, a whole clause
contrast: Mildly vulgar; avoid it at work or in writing. *Like crazy* is the polite version of the first sense.

senses.gloss: Very hard, very fast or very much.
examples: When the dog started barking, we ran *like hell*.
My knee hurts *like hell*.
They fought *like hell* to keep the factory open.

senses.gloss: Certainly not — a strong refusal or disbelief, at the front of a sentence.
examples: “You're paying for this.” “*Like hell* I am!”
*Like hell* he was sick — I saw him at the game.

type: manner — gradually
modifies: a verb or a whole clause

senses.gloss: Gradually, in small amounts or steps.
examples: *Little by little*, the town was rebuilt.
She's getting her strength back *little by little*.
Save a bit each month, and *little by little* it adds up.

type: time — a long time ago, and still true now
position: mid — usually with a perfect or passive verb (*has long since closed*)
contrast: *Since long* is not English (a calque of *с давних пор*): say *for a long time* or *long ago*.

senses.gloss: Long ago, with the result still true now.
examples: The factory has *long since* closed.
The old debts were *long since* paid off.
Those friends have *long since* moved away.

type: manner — the second-highest academic honor
comparison: not gradable — the three US honors, lowest to highest, are *cum laude*, *magna cum laude*, *summa cum laude*
contrast: Also used before a noun: *a magna cum laude graduate*.

senses.gloss: With high academic honors, above cum laude and below summa cum laude.
senses.ru: с отличием, с высокой академической наградой
examples: She graduated *magna cum laude* from Georgetown.
He finished *magna cum laude* with a degree in chemistry.
Only a handful of students in her class graduated *magna cum laude*.

ru: всё больше и больше, всё более
type: degree — increasingly
position: before its word — or end (*I like it more and more*)
contrast: With a one-syllable adjective, double the -er form: *colder and colder*, not *more and more cold*. Before a noun (*more and more people*) *more* is a determiner, not an adverb.

senses.gloss: Increasingly; to a growing degree.
senses.ru: всё больше и больше, всё более
examples: It's getting *more and more* difficult to find parking.
As the weeks passed, she missed home *more and more*.
The show got *more and more* ridiculous every season.

type: frequency — usually

senses.gloss: Usually; in most cases.
examples: *More often than not*, the bus is late.
He wins *more often than not*.
The forecast is wrong *more often than not*.

type: degree — approximately

senses.gloss: Almost; mostly, though not completely.
examples: The house is *more or less* finished.
I *more or less* agree with you.
We *more or less* got lost on the way.

senses.gloss: Approximately, with a number or amount.
examples: It'll cost two hundred dollars, *more or less*.
The drive takes an hour, *more or less*.

type: linking — marking the most important point
position: front — or before the last item in a list
modifies: a whole clause or the last item in a list
contrast: *Most important, …* is also correct, and some editors prefer it. Use *more importantly* when adding a second, bigger point to one already made.

senses.gloss: The most important thing is that.
examples: Pack water, a map and, *most importantly*, a charged phone.
*Most importantly*, nobody was hurt.
The new plan is cheaper, faster and, *most importantly*, safer.

ru: ноздря в ноздрю, голова в голову
type: manner — exactly even in a race or contest

senses.gloss: Exactly even in a race or competition.
examples: The two candidates are running *neck and neck* in the polls.
The horses came down the stretch *neck and neck*.
Sales of the two phones have been *neck and neck* all year.

type: place — in the next house, apartment or room
modifies: a verb, or a noun it follows (*the kids next door*)
contrast: *Next door* is the adverb; *next-door* with a hyphen is the adjective (*our next-door neighbors*); *next door to* works as a preposition (*She lives next door to us*).

senses.gloss: In or into the house, apartment or room beside this one.
examples: A young couple just moved in *next door*.
The kids *next door* are always playing basketball.
I ran *next door* to borrow some sugar.

type: stance — the speaker thinks something is very likely
contrast: Weaker than it looks: *No doubt you've heard the news* means *I suppose you have* (наверняка). For real certainty say *without a doubt* or *undoubtedly*.

senses.gloss: Probably; I am fairly sure.
examples: *No doubt* you've already heard the news.
He'll be late again, *no doubt*.
The team will *no doubt* be disappointed.

type: time — something that was true has stopped
contrast: *No longer* goes in mid position with a positive verb (*She no longer works here*); *not … anymore* goes at the end (*She doesn't work here anymore*). Never both: *She doesn't no longer work here* is wrong. Russian *больше не* tempts learners toward *no more*, which sounds literary here.

senses.gloss: Not now, though it was true before.
examples: She *no longer* works here.
The store is *no longer* open on Sundays.
I can *no longer* remember his name.

type: linking — adding a further point
position: end — before the item it adds
modifies: a noun, adjective or phrase added to the statement
contrast: Unlike *let alone*, it works after positive statements: *The hotel was expensive, not to mention noisy*.

senses.gloss: And also — adding something that makes the point stronger.
senses.ru: не говоря уже о, к тому же
examples: The house needs a new roof, *not to mention* new windows.
She speaks French and Spanish, *not to mention* a little Japanese.
Driving downtown costs a fortune in gas, *not to mention* parking.

type: frequency — occasionally
position: end — or front, often as *every now and again*
modifies: a verb or a whole clause

senses.gloss: Sometimes, but not regularly or often.
examples: We still have lunch together *now and again*.
*Now and again*, a car drove past the house.
It's fine to skip the gym *now and again*.

type: frequency — occasionally
position: end — or front, often as *every now and then*
modifies: a verb or a whole clause
contrast: *Now and again*, *every now and then* and *every so often* mean the same.

senses.gloss: Sometimes, but not often.
examples: I still see him *now and then*.
Every *now and then*, she calls to check on me.
It's nice to eat out *now and then*.

type: stance — the speaker treats something as expected or obvious
modifies: a whole clause, or stands alone as a reply
contrast: As a reply to a request it is warm (*Can I borrow a pen? — Of course*). As a reply to a question of fact it can sound like *obviously, you should know that*: *Is this your first time here? — Of course!* can come across as rude. Russian *конечно* is softer; for a neutral yes say *Sure* or *Yes, it is*.

senses.gloss: Certainly; as expected or as anyone would know.
examples: *Of course* you can bring a friend.
“Can you help me move on Saturday?” “*Of course*.”
He was late, *of course*, and blamed the traffic.

type: time — ever, in the whole of history
position: after its word — right after a superlative noun phrase
modifies: a noun phrase with a superlative (*the best … of all time*)
contrast: Russian *всех времён* is often rendered *of all times*; the English phrase is singular: *the greatest player of all time*. *Of all time* follows the noun; *ever* can follow it too (*the best movie ever*).

senses.gloss: Ever; in the whole of history — after a superlative.
examples: Many fans call him the greatest basketball player *of all time*.
It became the best-selling album *of all time*.
What's your favorite movie *of all time*?

type: time — recently; formal
modifies: a verb, usually in the present perfect
contrast: Formal; in speech Americans say *lately* or *recently*.

senses.gloss: Recently; in the last few weeks or months.
examples: Her health has been poor *of late*.
*Of late*, the company has been cutting costs.
He's been rather quiet *of late*.

type: manner — without preparation
contrast: Hyphenated before a noun: *an off-the-cuff remark*.

senses.gloss: Without preparing or thinking about it in advance.
examples: She spoke *off the cuff* for twenty minutes.
I'm just saying this *off the cuff*, so don't quote me.
The mayor answered the question *off the cuff*.

type: manner — unofficially, not for publication
modifies: verbs of speaking, or a whole clause
contrast: The opposite is *on the record* (официально, под запись). Hyphenated before a noun: *off-the-record comments*.

senses.gloss: Unofficially; not to be published or quoted.
examples: *Off the record*, the deal is already done.
The official spoke to reporters *off the record*.
Can I tell you something *off the record*?

type: manner — on hands and knees

senses.gloss: On the hands and knees.
examples: The baby crawled across the rug *on all fours*.
I was *on all fours* looking for my contact lens.
He got down *on all fours* so his daughter could ride on his back.

type: frequency — with breaks, not continuously
contrast: *Off and on* means the same. Before a noun: *an on-and-off relationship*, also *on-again, off-again*.

senses.gloss: At some times but not others, with breaks in between.
examples: It rained *on and off* all day.
They've been dating *on and off* for three years.
I worked there *on and off* during college.

type: viewpoint — as a typical or mean figure
modifies: a whole clause, often one with a number
contrast: *On the average* is the same, slightly older. Not *in average*, a common calque of *в среднем*.

senses.gloss: Usually, or as a typical amount when many cases are considered.
examples: *On average*, the trip takes about forty minutes.
Women live longer than men *on average*.
We get about three inches of rain a month *on average*.

type: place; also stance
contrast: Followed by a noun it works as a preposition (*on board the ship*). *Aboard* means the same in the first sense.

senses.gloss: On or in a ship, plane, train or bus.
examples: Once we were *on board*, the ferry left right away.
The captain made sure everyone was *on board*.
The flight attendants welcomed us *on board*.

senses.gloss: Part of a team, or in agreement with a plan.
examples: Is your boss *on board* with the idea?
We need the whole department *on board* before we announce it.
We're happy to have her *on board* as our new CFO.

type: degree — an intensifier in questions and negatives
position: after its word — right after *what*, *why*, *where*, *who*, *how*, or a negative noun phrase (*no reason on earth*)
modifies: a question word or a negative noun phrase
contrast: Shows surprise or annoyance: *What on earth…?* ≈ *Что же…? / Какого чёрта…?* *In the world* works the same way. In *the happiest man on earth* it is a literal phrase, not this adverb.

senses.gloss: Used after a question word or a negative to add surprise, annoyance or emphasis.
examples: What *on earth* are you doing?
Why *on earth* would anyone buy that?
There's no reason *on earth* to worry.

type: manner — without proof
position: end — usually in *take* or *accept something on faith*

senses.gloss: Without asking for proof; by trusting.
examples: I can't just take your word *on faith*; show me the numbers.
Most of us accept what doctors tell us *on faith*.
The investors took the founder's promises *on faith*.

type: frequency — sometimes, not often
modifies: a verb or a whole clause

senses.gloss: Sometimes, but not often.
examples: I still eat meat *on occasion*.
*On occasion*, the manager works the register herself.
He can be rude *on occasion*.

type: viewpoint — in theory or according to documents
contrast: Also literal: *put your thoughts on paper* (записать).

senses.gloss: According to documents or theory, though perhaps not in reality.
examples: *On paper*, it looked like the perfect plan.
He's a great candidate *on paper*, but the interview went badly.
The company is worth millions *on paper*.

type: manner — intentionally
contrast: Not *by purpose*. Russian *специально* has two meanings: *on purpose* (intentionally: *He broke it on purpose*) and *specially*, for one reason (*I came just to see you*).

senses.gloss: Intentionally; not by accident.
examples: He broke the vase *on purpose*!
Sorry, I didn't do it *on purpose*.
Did you leave the door open *on purpose*?

type: linking — rejecting what was said and stating the opposite
contrast: *On the contrary* rejects what was just said: *You're not bothering me — on the contrary, I'm glad you came* (наоборот). To compare two sides of one situation use *on the other hand* (с другой стороны). Mixing the two is a common learner error. *To the contrary* follows a noun: *despite rumors to the contrary*.

senses.gloss: Not at all — the opposite is true.
examples: “You must be bored.” “*On the contrary*, I'm having a great time.”
The medicine didn't help; *on the contrary*, it made him worse.
I don't dislike her. *On the contrary*, I think she's great.

type: time — exactly at the stated time
position: after its word — right after the clock time

senses.gloss: At exactly the stated time.
examples: The meeting starts at nine *on the dot*.
She showed up at noon *on the dot*.
The train left at 6:15 *on the dot*.

ru: на первый взгляд, судя по всему
type: viewpoint — judging by how things appear

senses.gloss: Judging by how something looks at first, which may not be the whole truth.
examples: *On the face of it*, the offer looks generous.
*On the face of it*, the two cases have nothing in common.
It seems, *on the face of it*, like a simple mistake.

type: manner — while something is already happening

senses.gloss: Quickly, while something is already in progress, without planning ahead.
examples: We didn't have a plan, so we made decisions *on the fly*.
The app translates speech *on the fly*.
Good teachers adjust the lesson *on the fly*.

type: degree — exactly
position: after its word — right after a time or amount, or at the end
modifies: a time, an amount, or a verb
contrast: As an adjective phrase it also means *too obvious, not subtle*: *The movie's message was a little on the nose*.

senses.gloss: Exactly; precisely.
examples: She guessed the final score *on the nose*.
The bill came to fifty dollars *on the nose*.
We arrived at eight *on the nose*.

type: linking — introducing the first of two contrasting points
contrast: Normally followed by *on the other hand*; *on one hand* without *the* is also common in American English.

senses.gloss: Introducing the first of two different or opposing points.
examples: *On the one hand*, the job pays well; on the other hand, the hours are long.
*On the one hand*, I'd love to travel. On the other, I hate flying.
I'm torn: *on the one hand*, I trust him; on the other, the facts don't add up.

type: linking — introducing a contrasting point
contrast: It adds another side of the same situation, not a correction; to reject what was said use *on the contrary* (наоборот). It is often used alone, without *on the one hand*.

senses.gloss: Introducing a different or opposite side of the same situation.
examples: The city is exciting. *On the other hand*, it's very expensive.
My brother loves sports; I, *on the other hand*, would rather read.
It's a great car. *On the other hand*, we can't really afford it.

type: manner
modifies: a verb, or a noun it follows (*fries on the side*)

senses.gloss: In addition to one's main job or relationship, often secretly.
examples: He does repair work *on the side*.
She's a nurse but sells jewelry *on the side*.
He'd been seeing someone *on the side* for months.

senses.gloss: Served separately, not on top of the main food.
examples: Could I get the dressing *on the side*?
The steak comes with fries *on the side*.

type: manner — secretly

senses.gloss: Secretly, so that others don't notice.
examples: He's been smoking *on the sly*.
She read her sister's diary *on the sly*.
They were meeting *on the sly* after work.

ru: сразу, на месте; в затруднительное положение
type: time; also place
modifies: a verb, or a noun it follows (*a reporter on the spot*)
contrast: British *run on the spot* is *run in place* in American English.

senses.gloss: Immediately, right then and there.
examples: He was fired *on the spot*.
They offered me the job *on the spot*.
The officer wrote him a ticket *on the spot*.

senses.gloss: In a difficult position where one must answer or act at once — usually *put someone on the spot*.
examples: The reporter's question really put the senator *on the spot*.
Sorry to put you *on the spot*, but could you say a few words?

senses.gloss: At the place where something is happening.
examples: Paramedics were *on the spot* within minutes.
Our reporter *on the spot* has the latest.
